## Eight big questions about your brain and AI.

The original compilation, with narration and illustrations. Choose a chapter below, or watch straight through. The film loads only when you press play.

CHOOSE A CHAPTER · TAP TO WATCH

These films start with a question entered into Drift, the free idea-mapping app . The map is a starting point, not a scientific authority. This reading companion separates useful explanations from hypotheses and adds research checked on September 30, 2026.

## Why does time seem to speed up?

Your memory is not a stopwatch.

There are two different questions: how long a moment feels while you live it , and how much time it seems to contain when you remember it . Attention matters to the first. Changes in place, activity and goals help organize the second into distinct episodes.

A March 2026 experiment with 32 fMRI participants found that items separated by a context change were remembered as farther apart. It supports a memory mechanism, not a complete explanation of aging. The familiar “a year is a smaller fraction of your life” idea is an intuition, not an established law of perception. Read the experiment (2026) ↗

Give this week one distinct landmark: a new route, a skill, an unhurried conversation. Write a sentence about it afterward. Treat it as a memory experiment, not a promise to slow time.

## Why is doomscrolling hard to stop?

An endless feed removes the moment to choose.

A feed can combine alarming information, occasional rewards and frictionless continuation. That makes “just one more” easy. The slot-machine comparison is a useful analogy, but it is not a diagnosis or a complete account of everyone's behavior.

Foundational research linked social posting to reward learning, including a 176-person experiment . It studied social rewards and posting behavior, not every mechanism of doomscrolling. The distinction matters. Read the study (2021) ↗

Decide what you came to find before opening the feed. Use one deliberate stopping cue: a timer, a fixed reading list, or autoplay switched off. Put the choice back into the interface.

## How does the brain run on about 20 watts?

A commonly cited estimate of whole-brain metabolic power. Not the energy cost of one thought.

Brains weave memory and processing together and use activity patterns very differently from conventional computers. Those are useful design clues. But the brain still spends considerable energy sending signals and maintaining cells. It is not a free computer with no data-movement costs. Read the energy accounting (2021) ↗

Comparing one brain with a whole AI data center mixes different systems, workloads and numbers of users. A meaningful comparison needs the same task, accuracy, speed and full energy boundary. There is no honest single “brains are X times more efficient” number here.

Ask how much data must move and how much work can be skipped. Efficiency is a systems problem, not just a faster-chip problem.

## Why can learning something new erase old skills?

Updating shared weights can help one task and hurt another.

That interference is called catastrophic forgetting . It is a risk, not a rule that all AI updates must fail. Also separate three kinds of “learning”: using the current conversation, retrieving saved information, and changing the model's weights. They are not interchangeable.

### Learning 100 tasks, then testing what remains

Average final retention across three memorization datasets.

A different September 20 preprint updated six open-weight models on later web data. Five improved on older factual recall as well. Different data and evaluation produced a different result. “AI cannot keep learning” is too absolute.

When a system claims to learn continuously, ask: what changed, which old skills were retested, and what was lost? A saved chat is not proof of improved model weights.

## Why do we dream?

We have clues, not one settled purpose.

Dreams occur in REM and non-REM sleep. Sleep supports memory processes, but that does not establish that the dream you remember is itself doing memory consolidation. Dreaming across sleep stages (2017) ↗

Erik Hoel's 2021 hypothesis suggests strange dreams might help us generalize beyond repetitive experience, like varied training examples help a model. It remains a hypothesis. A July 2026 mouse study measured changing energy dynamics in REM sleep; it did not establish the function of human dreams.

A compelling analogy is a way to ask better questions. It is not evidence that brains and language models work in the same way.

## Could AI discover new physics?

Finding a formula is a start. Nature still gets a vote.

Symbolic regression searches for compact equations that fit observations. A formula can fit the available data and still fail outside it. For the film's simple example, d = ½at² assumes constant acceleration, zero initial velocity and zero initial displacement.

A July 2026 preprint compared ways of using language models across 74 known physics equations and seven harder formula-recovery tasks . Guiding the numerical search worked best in that comparison. Recovering known equations is not the discovery of a new law of nature.

Whenever an AI-generated explanation sounds impressive, ask what new observation would distinguish it from the alternatives. If nothing could prove it wrong, you do not yet have a useful scientific claim.

For a real decision, the next question is not just “Can AI do this?” It is “What changes for my direction?” Private consulting brings that wider view to your own situation.

## Why does AI tell you that you are right?

A pleasing answer is not necessarily a true answer.

Sycophancy means excessive agreement or flattery. Preference training can reward agreeable answers, and the way you frame a question can steer the response. But “AI always agrees” is an overstatement, and not every friendly reply is sycophancy.

Across 30 decision environments, AI advice moved people away from initial leanings on average, despite measured sycophancy. More sycophancy weakened that effect. The decision study ↗

Two experiments found that warnings and demonstrations changed how people evaluated a sycophantic chatbot, but did not reduce its persuasiveness. The awareness study ↗

These findings address different tasks and outcomes. Together they caution against both trusting agreement and assuming every AI conversation makes judgment worse.

“Evaluate the evidence before considering my preference. Give the strongest counterargument, identify uncertainties, and tell me what would change your conclusion.” Then verify important claims outside the chat. A prompt is not a safety guarantee.

## Why can you recognize a face but not explain how?

Being able to do something is not the same as describing it.

Face recognition integrates features and their arrangement. Inverting a face disrupts recognition disproportionately. Research links this effect to spatial processing in face-selective brain regions. There is no single little “face rule” available for conscious inspection. Read the study (2021) ↗

This illustrates tacit knowledge : skills can exceed our ability to state their workings. It does not mean face recognition is beyond scientific explanation, or that a successful AI classifier understands faces exactly as humans do.

When teaching a hard-to-describe skill, show good and bad examples and compare them. Then test on a new case. A fluent explanation and reliable performance are two different things.

FROM WATCHING TO EXPLORING

## One question. Three moves.

- Start narrow. “Why do familiar weeks feel short in memory?” is more useful than “Explain time.”

- Go Deeper, then Wander. Understand one mechanism. Then follow a neighboring idea or a competing explanation.

- Check what matters. Keep observations, hypotheses and analogies separate. Open the original research before trusting a number.

The recorded maps grew to 10 ideas in seven examples and 16 in the time example. Those are counts of generated nodes, not counts of verified facts . More branches are valuable only when they improve your understanding.

No account or API key needed. AI can be wrong; leave out personal or confidential information.

## The Reach of Being

A narration-only film that travels from a hand stencil at least 67,800 years old to a 2025 model that turned text prompts into worlds you could move through.

CHOOSE A MOMENT · TAP TO WATCH

## We already live a little beyond our skin.

We choose glasses, borrow a gesture from someone we admire, arrange a room until it feels like ours. Something inward takes an outward form, and then we live inside it.

Spectacles show how quickly a tool becomes part of a self. In a Florence sermon from early 1306 by modern reckoning, the friar Giordano da Pisa said the art of making them was not yet twenty years old. They began as a way to see. At a mirror today, the question is also: is this me?

> “In time, we begin to inhabit what we have made.”

Research: the 1306 sermon Reflection: living inside what we make

## Every reach comes with a limit.

Tools are older than we are: flaked stones from Lomekwi 3, in northern Kenya, are about 3.3 million years old, far older than our species. Here are four later stops from the film, each paired with what the evidence does not say.

How claims are marked Research Reflection Speculation Imagined

LIANG METANDUNO · MUNA, SULAWESI · AT LEAST 67,800 YEARS

### A hand that left, an outline that stayed

Someone pressed a hand to the rock and sprayed pigment around it. The outline stayed. Later, its fingers were deliberately narrowed into a claw-like shape. What that meant remains open.

The date is a minimum, not a moment of creation. Calcite that formed over the stencil dates to about 71,600 years, give or take 3,800, so the stencil is at least 67,800 years old. Its maker is unknown. A trace keeps the outline of a hand, not the life behind it.

Research Reflection: the last line

MACAQUES, 1996 · PEOPLE, 2009

### A tool can enter the body’s map

After macaques learned to rake in objects out of reach, neurons that responded to touch on the hand and to sights near it began responding along the rake. After people used a mechanical grabber, their free-hand movements and localization of touches changed, consistent with a longer represented arm.

These are changes in how the brain represents the body for a task, not physical growth. The monkey recordings came during tool use and the human measures after it; this note makes no claim about how long the effect lasts. Neither study is evidence about AI minds.

Research, historical studies

ENGLAND · 1363

### A mark that answers for the work

From 1363, English goldsmiths had to strike a mark of their own on their wares. An object could now carry its maker into rooms the maker would never enter.

The rule required a mark that identified the maker. Reading it as “and answers for it” is the film’s interpretation. It is also the useful part: the further work travels without us, the more it needs a name that can be found.

Research Reflection: answerability

KALOBEYEI · TURKANA, KENYA · DESIGNED C. 2017 · FIRST SPACE BUILT 2018

### A game world that stepped off the screen

Refugees and host community members learned design skills in Minecraft in workshops with UN-Habitat and the Block by Block Foundation, then planned shared public spaces. The plan provided for shade, solar lighting and more than 500 trees. Women had major roles in building the space and planting.

Software did not build the place. People did, with partners including UNHCR, the Turkana County Government and AAR Japan. In December 2018, UN-Habitat reported one of four spaces and a transport hub built, with the other three due to start in 2019.

Research

Each time, intention travels further from the body. Each time, someone still has to choose it, build it, sign it and look after it.

## What was possible in 2025, and what it does not prove.

The film suggests AI may widen this radius, perhaps exponentially: an idea becoming a working system, an imagined place becoming somewhere others can enter. That part is speculation. Two dated results give it texture, not proof.

Speculation: “perhaps exponentially”

### Longer tasks, on a human clock

METR measured a software task’s length by how long it takes a human professional. The length of tasks frontier AI agents could complete about half the time had doubled roughly every seven months over the previous six years. The report put Claude 3.7 Sonnet at about an hour.

Not a forecast, and not a measure of today’s systems, their speed or their intelligence. The authors name real-world transfer among their main uncertainties.

### A world from a text prompt

Genie 3 generated environments from text that a user could move through in real time, at 24 frames per second and 720p, staying consistent for a few minutes.

A limited research preview, with a limited action space, short interactions and imperfect real-world accuracy. The harbor in the film is a drawing, not model footage.

The film pictures a teacher describing a tide pool to an AI system, then shaping it with students into a small world they can explore: tap a crab, raise the tide, see what survives. Contrast it with Kalobeyei, which really happened and was built by people on the ground.

Two boundaries keep this honest. A doubling trend on particular tasks is not a law of nature. And the body-map research above concerns rakes and grabbers. It does not show that AI systems have minds, or that software becomes part of your body.

Reflection: the boundaries

## A faster tool does not make a wiser hand.

Making more is not the same as meaning more. As ideas become working systems more easily, the scarce part shifts away from making and toward the crafts the film calls old:

- Choose what deserves to exist. Ten generated options are not ten decisions. With abundance, selection becomes the skill.

- Mark what you made. A modern maker’s mark can be a plain note: who made this, with which tools, and what was checked.

- Answer for it. What others meet is a partial shape of you, and it can help or harm them. Stay findable when it does.

- Maintain it. A world others can enter needs someone who keeps it working after the excitement fades, and who retires it with care.

Reflection: the film’s argument, not a finding

## Four questions before you extend yourself.

Use this before you hand a task to an agent, publish a tool, or open a space to other people. There is no score. The value is in writing honest answers somewhere you will see them again.

Imagined example An agent that drafts replies to customer emails.

- What am I extending? Which part of my intention, effort or presence should travel further? Example Fast, consistent first drafts, so people hear back sooner.

Which part of my intention, effort or presence should travel further?

Example Fast, consistent first drafts, so people hear back sooner.

- What am I preserving? What stays in my own hands, voice or attention? Example Refunds, apologies, and anything that turns on a relationship.

What stays in my own hands, voice or attention?

Example Refunds, apologies, and anything that turns on a relationship.

- Who bears the consequences? Who meets this when I am not there, and who inherits it later? Example A customer who gets a confident wrong answer. Whoever maintains the agent next year.

Who meets this when I am not there, and who inherits it later?

Example A customer who gets a confident wrong answer. Whoever maintains the agent next year.

- What deserves my attention? What will I check, and how often, after the excitement fades? Example Read a sample of sent replies every Friday. Review everything it escalates.
